indicators.note: A hug closes right around whatever it takes hold of, so one word here wraps itself about another instead of sitting beside it.

parts.note: a longing is a desire, and it parts after its fourth letter
if you cannot bear a person you cannot stand them

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to picture hugging a bear. 'Bear' is really the verb meaning put up with, and the hug is one word opening to let another in.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-established → LONG-STANDING: a long-standing arrangement has held its place for years, settled by sheer age rather than by rank.

clue.text: Engage in combat using bolt and car parts

parts.note: a bolt slid across a door is one kind of lock
the horn is the part of a car you sound, and the plural fills the second word

explanation.walkthrough: Two stags jamming their antlers together is where the phrase comes from, so 'car parts' has to work hard to keep you thinking about a garage instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Engage in combat → LOCK HORNS: the idiom for two parties fighting it out, borrowed from rutting stags whose antlers jam together.

clue.text: Managed to rise and judge first of defendants chronicled

indicators.note: Whatever rises travels upwards, and in a down entry upwards means the letters are written back the way they came.

parts.note: managed a shop = RAN it, and this down entry reads those letters up the column
to judge a performance is to rate it

indicators.note: The first of any group stands at its head, so the word behind this surrenders nothing but its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter of Defendants

explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts a courtroom on its feet while the clue quietly stacks three pieces. RATE for judge is worth banking — it appears whenever a clue mentions marking or scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: chronicled → NARRATED: to narrate is to give an account of events in order, which is what a chronicle does; both are past-tense verbs.

clue.text: Son caught in the morning with first of scarpering cons

indicators.note: Being first of a set means standing at its front, so the word that follows gives up only its leading letter.

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
C is how a catch is recorded on a cricket scorecard
ante meridiem, the morning half of the clock
the leading letter of Scarpering

explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught in the morning' sounds like a single idea and is really two abbreviations laid side by side. Four separate pieces for five letters is the Quiptic being generous.
explanation.definitionFit: cons → SCAMS: a con is a swindle worked by gaining trust, and a scam is the same trick under its shorter, more modern slang name.

indicators.note: Whatever happens during an event happens inside it, so one piece goes in the middle of the other rather than after it.

parts.note: the four letters of DATE resettled, then parted to make room

indicators.note: Unusual means not in its usual state, and letters not in their usual state are letters not in their usual order.

parts.note: to allure somebody is to tempt them

explanation.walkthrough: A date that reads as a romantic evening is only four letters of material, and the longest word in the clue is the one that ends up buried in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Tried → ATTEMPTED: both are past-tense verbs for having a go at something — tried as in 'tried to reach him', not tried in court.

indicators.note: An embrace closes around what it holds, and the 'by' settles which of the two words does the holding.

parts.note: a dean runs a cathedral chapter
the person setting the puzzle calls themselves ME, one of the oldest crossword conventions

explanation.walkthrough: 'Humble' is the verb here rather than the adjective, which is the whole difficulty. The setter turning up inside a word as ME is worth banking for good.
explanation.definitionFit: Humble → DEMEAN: to demean someone is to lower them in other people's eyes, the transitive verb 'humble' rather than the modest adjective.

indicators.note: Coming after something means coming along behind it, so the journalist's two letters are parked at the back of the chain.

parts.note: the plainest negative answer in the language
T is the standard abbreviation for time, as in a physics formula
an editor is the journalist crosswords always reach for

explanation.walkthrough: The clue has to be read back to front: its last two words are the first letters of the answer. ED for a journalist is standing crossword vocabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrated → NOTED: a noted scholar is a celebrated one — the adjective meaning widely known, not the past tense of writing something down.

clue.text: Try and go up for idle chat

indicators.note: In a down entry, letters that go up are read from the foot of the column to the top, which turns the word round.

parts.note: a try at something is a go at it
'go' is the household euphemism for PISS, and a down entry reads those four letters upwards

explanation.walkthrough: The same little word does two different jobs a few letters apart: once as an ordinary synonym, once as the euphemism small children are taught.
explanation.definitionFit: idle chat → GOSSIP: talk about other people's private business, idle in the sense that it serves no purpose beyond the telling.

indicators.note: Various means taking more than one form, and material that can take more than one form is material waiting to be rearranged.
Here 'left' is the past tense of leaving rather than the direction, and what leaves a word is gone from it.

parts.note: the seven letters the wordplay starts from
love is nothing in tennis, written as a nought, and it is the letter that departs

explanation.walkthrough: Take a word, drop a letter, rearrange the rest. Love for O comes from the tennis score and is one of the most useful conventions there is.
explanation.definitionFit: traps → SNARES: a snare is a wire noose set to catch an animal, and by extension any trap laid for the unwary.

parts.note: love is nothing in tennis, and nothing is written as a nought
a scar is the mark an old wound leaves behind

explanation.walkthrough: The capital M makes 'Mark' look like somebody's name when it is an ordinary noun — a trick setters use whenever a word doubles as a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: award → OSCAR: definition by example — the Academy's gold statuette standing in for the general word for a prize.

clue.text: Fruit held by gold, new clockwork device

indicators.note: To be held by something is to be kept inside its grip, so the fruit sits within the other letters rather than in front of them.

parts.note: AU is gold's symbol on the periodic table
botanically a fruit, whatever the salad suggests
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.walkthrough: The comma is the disguise: 'gold, new' looks like a description of the device and is really two abbreviations with the long word wedged between them.
explanation.definitionFit: clockwork device → AUTOMATON: a self-moving mechanical figure, historically driven by clockwork — a machine built to imitate something living.

clue.text: Sleeps following second cold then hot drink

indicators.note: What follows comes along behind, so the word standing at the front of the clue lands at the back of the answer.

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for a second of time
C is the letter on the cold tap
H is the letter on the hot tap
someone who sleeps briefly in the afternoon naps

explanation.walkthrough: The German spelling takes a single P, so check it against the crossing letters. C and H are the pair of letters on a set of taps, and both turn up constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: drink → SCHNAPS: definition by example — the strong colourless German spirit served in small glasses, one liquor standing for the general word.

indicators.note: Doing a thing wrongly is doing it other than as it should be done, and letters other than as they should be are letters out of order.

parts.note: seven letters that resettle into the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Snake' is a verb here — a river snakes through a valley — and the noun at the front of a clue is always the cheapest misdirection a setter has.
explanation.definitionFit: Snake → MEANDER: to meander is to wind in slow loops the way a lowland river does, which is what a road or stream is said to snake.

clue.text: Preserve and tea peer put out

indicators.note: A thing out of true is a thing not where it belongs, so the letters in front of this word are knocked from their places.

parts.note: ten letters, exactly the length the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: Counting is the way in here. The surface reads as an affronted aristocrat — 'put out' also means offended — while the three words in the middle are simply material.
explanation.definitionFit: Preserve → PERPETUATE: to perpetuate something is to keep it going indefinitely, preserving it in existence rather than in vinegar.

indicators.note: To doctor a document is to tamper with it, and letters tampered with no longer sit in the order they were handed to you.

parts.note: nine letters that rearrange into the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a second character standing beside the nun and is really the instruction. Verbs meaning tamper — doctor, cook, fix — are the anagram signals to learn first.
explanation.definitionFit: Simple → UNADORNED: plain and carrying no decoration, simple in the sense of undecorated rather than easy or foolish.

clue.text: Leaders of legal establishment start speechifying to a smaller degree

indicators.note: A leader goes at the front of whatever it leads, so each word in the run behind gives up only the character at its head.

parts.note: the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Legal establishment' reads as one idea, which is how the setter hides two of the four initials inside a single phrase. Four words in a row is the tell.
explanation.definitionFit: to a smaller degree → LESS: the comparative adverb — 'less inclined' means inclined to a smaller degree — rather than the quantity word before a noun.

clue.text: Left Charlie out for line to be judged

indicators.note: Sending one thing out for another is a swap, so the letter named first leaves and the letter named second takes over its place.

parts.note: a building left in a hurry has been evacuated
Charlie is C in the radio alphabet, and it is the letter that goes
L is the standard abbreviation for line, and it moves in

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a single letter away from a word meaning left. Radio-alphabet names — Charlie, Oscar, Romeo, Victor — always stand for one letter each.
explanation.definitionFit: to be judged → EVALUATED: to evaluate is to weigh a thing up and set a value on it, judging its worth rather than its guilt.

clue.text: Small cross is reformed as cutting instrument

definitions.note: Scissors is one of those tools English only ever names in the plural, like tongs and pliers, so the singular 'instrument' is the natural way to define the single object.

indicators.note: To reform a thing is to form it again in a new shape, and letters formed again come out in a different arrangement.

parts.note: S is the label on the smallest size of shirt
seven letters more, which with the S make the eight wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'is' as grammar. It is material, and once you count it in, the letter count matches the enumeration exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: cutting instrument → SCISSORS: the two pivoted blades you cut paper or cloth with, an implement named only by the pair of them.

parts.note: B is the bishop in chess notation
to question somebody is to ask them

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue tells you to add the pieces up: it simply sets them side by side, which is how the plainest charades work. B for bishop comes from chess.
explanation.definitionFit: lie → BASK: to bask is to lie stretched out in warmth or sunshine, the verb you would use of a cat on a windowsill.

parts.note: bud is the American way of addressing a mate
to obtain a thing is to get it

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are everyday words, so all the difficulty lies in seeing where to cut. Deciding that 'Mate' means friend, not spouse or chess move, is the first step.
explanation.definitionFit: spending allowance → BUDGET: the sum set aside for what may be spent in a period, whether by a household or a chancellor.

clue.text: Workmanship shown by worker in charge a lot

parts.note: a farm hand or a deck hand is a worker
IC is how the officer in charge is written on a duty roster
a raft of measures is a great many of them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' is the crossword's favourite ambiguity — ANT, BEE or HAND, decided by the letter count. 'A raft of' for a large number is worth banking as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Workmanship → HANDICRAFT: skilled making done by hand, so the word covers both the trade itself and the quality of what it turns out.

definitions.meaning: the everyday word for a banknote of that value, as heard in casual requests to borrow one
this entry is number 20 in the grid, so its own label is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The second half looks as though it defines nothing, because it points at the clue itself rather than at the world. Self-reference like this is rare and always worth checking for.
explanation.definitionFit: Note → TWENTY: a twenty is the banknote of that value, and this entry's own number in the grid is 20.

indicators.note: Things lying about are lying anyhow rather than in their proper places, which is what happens to the three letters in front of it.

parts.note: a mob is a disorderly crowd
the three letters of LIE strewn into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: A British mobile is what an American calls a cell, so 'phone' alone is the definition. Three letters barely disturbed are the hardest kind of rearrangement to notice.
explanation.definitionFit: phone → MOBILE: the British name for a handset you carry about, short for mobile phone and now standing on its own as a noun.

clue.text: Old boa I reshaped into circus prop

indicators.note: Anything reshaped keeps its material and loses its form, so the same letters come back in a different arrangement.

parts.note: seven letters, the exact length of the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The snake and the feather stole are both decoys — 'boa' is here for its three letters. A stray 'I' swept into the material is a standard way of making the count work.
explanation.definitionFit: circus prop → DIABOLO: the double-cone spool spun and thrown on a string between two sticks, a staple of juggling acts.

parts.note: the clue's own opening word, taken at face value
corn is seed grain, the kernel sown in a field

explanation.walkthrough: Three words with nothing to spare: a letter, a synonym and a definition. Short clues hide their join because 'A seed' reads so naturally as one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: fruit → ACORN: the fruit of the oak in the botanical sense, where a nut counts as a fruit even though nobody puts one in a bowl.

parts.note: beyond the church means past it
the Ure runs through Wensleydale, one of the short rivers crosswords rely on

explanation.walkthrough: Rivers are the crossword's favourite three-letter filler — Ure, Exe, Cam, Dee, Po — and the bare word 'river' is the usual signal to reach for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Meadow → PASTURE: grassland kept for animals to graze, the same sort of field a meadow is, named from the farmer's side of it.

definitions.meaning: the throb you feel at the wrist is the beat of the blood
beans, peas and lentils belong to a crop family that carries this same name

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and a question mark. The mark is the setter admitting the second definition is only an example, since a bean is one kind of the answer rather than the whole class.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat → PULSE: the throb of blood at the wrist; and a pulse is the edible seed of a legume, which 'bean?' defines by naming one.

indicators.note: To upset a tray is to spill everything arranged on it, so what follows lands in a heap instead of in the order given.

parts.note: nine letters that resettle as the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' does double duty: it describes the state of the person the answer fits and instructs you to disturb the letters. 'Too' is material, not an intensifier.
explanation.definitionFit: sensitive → EMOTIONAL: quick to feel and to show feeling, sensitive in the sense of easily moved rather than easily damaged.

clue.text: College note in books for group

indicators.note: Putting a thing in something puts it inside, so these letters go between the two the books supply rather than after them.

parts.note: the Old Testament, the books crosswords mean when they say books
C is the abbreviation for college, as written in an address
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.walkthrough: 'Books' is nearly always one Testament or the other, with the crossing letters deciding which. Sol-fa supplies the notes: do, re, mi, fa, so, la, te.
explanation.definitionFit: group → OCTET: a group of exactly eight, usually musicians playing together — the number is what the word adds to the definition.

clue.text: Renders dudes drunk and overly casual

indicators.note: Somebody drunk cannot hold a straight line, and letters that cannot hold their line arrive in any order at all.

parts.note: twelve letters, exactly the length of the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Drunk is the commonest anagram signal there is, and here it also carries the surface: dudes at a party, turned out for a different one entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: overly casual → UNDERDRESSED: dressed below what the occasion called for, casual where something smarter was expected.
